newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Subdued Irish inflation seen easing rate rise fear.
newsitem.headline: Subdued Irish inflation seen easing rate rise fear.

text.p: Lower-than-expected May Irish inflation data should reassure the central bank that recent Irish pound weakness, a booming economy and strong lending growth have not fed through to price inflation - yet.
Analysts said on Friday that the data removed any prospect of an imminent interest rate rise but they warned that Ireland was not out of the woods on the inflation front.
Ireland's May consumer price index rose by 0.2 percent on April and was up 1.5 percent year-on-year, at the lower end of market expectations.
"It's definitely a better number than anybody expected. Generally, it's very subdued, there is absolutely no currency effect in this," Dermot O'Brien, economist at NCB Stockbrokers told Reuters.
He noted that wholesale prices, which are usually sensitive to the gyrations in the Irish pound's trade-weighted index, had risen far less than expected in May.
Producer prises rose 0.4 percent on the month and fell 1.5 percent year-on-year despite a sharp drop in the value of the Irish pound last month.
"If it's not coming through at the wholesale level, then there's absolutely no reason to expect it come through to the CPI," O'Brien said.

Analysts said there was no way the central bank would now raise rates but a disappointing number, following on the heels of last week's strong lending data, would have triggered fears in the market of a rate rise.
"We should see a positive effect on the short end of the market," said Pat O'Sullivan, economist at AIB Group Treasury. "You should see cash rates coming off slightly, maybe by about a 1/16."
Analysts said the data should also help the bond market at the margin.

"It's continued confirmation of a low inflation rate despite the fact that there is strong growth forecast," said NCB's O'Brien, who also noted that the harmonised index of consumer prices, used for intra-EU comparison, showed Ireland well on course to meet the inflation criteria for Economic and monetary union (EMU).
But analysts warned that there could be trouble on the inflation front further down the line, particularly if the Irish pound remains weak.

"While price pressures are under control for the moment, the Central Bank are still worried about the longer term trend particularly with domestic credit demand remaining high and the Irish pound looking vulnerable against its main trading partners," Alan McQuaid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers, said.
AIB's O'Sullivan said he expected inflation to drift up toward end of year and said higher interest rates could be on the cards.

"The central bank know the weakness of the currency is going to feed through into the inflation numbers, the economy is still growing strongly, the credit numbers are strong. If the currency does weaken, higher rates are in prospect," he said.
